newsitem.title: USA: Comair grew from small carrier to regional force.
newsitem.headline: Comair grew from small carrier to regional force.

text.p: The Comair crash near Detroit was only the second fatal mishap in the history of an airline that has grown from a small operation to a major regional force in 19 years.
Comair began by serving only Detroit, Cleveland, Cincinnati and Akron, Ohio. Today it has about 660 flights daily to 79 cities in 26 states, Canada and the Bahamas.

In 1979, eight people were killed when a Piper Navajo crashed on takeoff from the airline's hub, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport. The cause of that crash was never determined, a Comair spokeswoman said.

A securities analyst who follows the company, Mark Koprucki of the Ohio Co. in Columbus, Ohio, said "Comair has an excellent safety record. I know management very well, and they are adamant about flight safety."
Founded in 1977, Comair has 92 jets and turboprop airplanes. The plane that went down on approach to Detroit Thursday was a turboprop Brasilia 120, built by Brazil-based Embraer SA.

It was one of 40 such planes in the Comair fleet, a spokeswoman said. The 30-seat airplane in the accident was delivered new to Comair in February 1992 and had its most recent major overhaul on Nov. 20, 1996, Comair said.
Comair said it had been replacing turboprops to provide better service.
It has 45 Canadian-built Canadair regional jets built by Bombardier Inc. as well as eight soon-to-retire Saab SF-340 turboprops. Five more Canadairs are on order.
Thursday's crash occurred in late afternoon during snow and winds but there has been no confirmation that weather was a factor.
Comair calls itself the "Delta Connection." Its flights connect with flights of Atlanta-based Delta Air Lines, Inc., which owns about 20 percent of Comair stock, Comair said.

In fiscal 1996, ended in March, Comair Holdings, Inc., the parent company, doubled net earnings from 1995 to $60 million, or $1.36 a share (reflecting a three-for-two stock split in May 1996). Revenues rose 29 percent to $463 million.
